paragraphs: Regression trees estimate a relationship by dividing the input space into regions and fitting local predictions. This paper investigates the statistical behavior of Bayesian versions of that strategy in a specific setting: regression with one predictor, where the true relationship is constant between jumps and the number of jumps is unknown.

The authors study Bayesian regression histograms, including dyadic trees, and show that suitably chosen prior distributions lead the posterior to concentrate near the true function at a nearly optimal worst-case rate. Crucially, the procedure does not need advance knowledge of how many constant pieces exist or how wide their intervals are.

The result gives a precise sense in which these trees adapt to unknown complexity: they recover the function nearly as well as a procedure informed about the jumps. This is an initial theoretical explanation for Bayesian trees' practical success within the studied setting. The paper also connects priors over balanced interval partitions to a geometric probability problem involving random arcs covering a circle.
neurips-2017-bayesian-dyadic-trees-and-h.tldr: With suitable priors, Bayesian dyadic regression trees adapt to unknown steps in a one-predictor regression function at a near-optimal rate.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering makes recommendations using patterns in historical data, but those patterns can reflect discrimination. The paper examines how this can produce unfair predictions for minority users. Its starting point is that assessing a recommender requires attention to how it treats different groups, and that existing fairness metrics do not adequately capture the relevant problems.

The authors introduce four metrics intended to capture different forms of unfairness. Having several objectives makes fairness assessment more specific: different measures can reveal different ways predictions disadvantage users. The paper also connects measurement to training by adding terms based on these metrics to the learning objective, allowing fairness considerations to influence the model being fitted.

Experiments with synthetic and real data find that the proposed metrics measure fairness better than the evaluated baseline and that optimizing the associated objectives reduces unfairness. The contribution therefore combines a way to assess unequal treatment with a way to address it during learning. The reported improvement concerns the forms of unfairness these objectives measure.
neurips-2017-beyond-parity-fairness-obje.tldr: Four fairness metrics and corresponding training objectives help identify and reduce unfair predictions in collaborative-filtering recommenders.

paragraphs: Markov jump processes describe systems that change state at random times in continuous time. Inferring their hidden behavior commonly involves Markov chain Monte Carlo, which can be computationally challenging. This paper develops a variational alternative that approximates the distribution of possible trajectories through an optimization problem.

The method uses uniformization, a connection between continuous-time jump processes and discrete-time Markov chains. It first integrates out the process parameters, which is the collapsing step. It then approximates the remaining trajectory distribution using a factored distribution over segments of a function that stays constant between changes. This shifts the inference problem toward a structured representation of the trajectory.

A central distinction is how time is handled. Whereas the compared MCMC schemes integrate out transition times, this algorithm optimizes the time discretization, yielding substantial computational savings. On synthetic data and a dataset of check-in recordings, the authors report better performance than leading MCMC methods. These findings support the proposed combination of parameter marginalization and trajectory approximation as an efficient inference strategy.
neurips-2017-collapsed-variational-bayes.tldr: A collapsed variational method accelerates inference for Markov jump processes by integrating out parameters and optimizing the time discretization.

paragraphs: A Gaussian mixture represents data using several Gaussian components, each with its own center and share of the mixture. This paper analyzes the gradient version of expectation-maximization for fitting such models. It covers an arbitrary number of components and mixing coefficients, extending beyond the simpler case of two symmetric components.

The authors derive a convergence rate that explicitly depends on the mixture weights, the smallest and largest distances between true centers, the data dimension, and the number of components. These dependencies explain how the statistical configuration enters the algorithm's convergence behavior. They also obtain a nearly optimal local contraction radius, describing a neighborhood where updates move toward the target.

The local nature of the result matters: it characterizes convergence near the true solution rather than claiming success from every initialization. Handling multiple components and general weights requires structurally different arguments from the two-component symmetric case. The analysis draws on learning theory and empirical-process tools to establish guarantees for this broader family of mixture models.
neurips-2017-convergence-of-gradient-em-.tldr: The paper establishes local convergence guarantees for gradient EM with general multi-component Gaussian mixtures.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering seeks groups in data through their underlying representational structure. This paper builds an unsupervised neural architecture around a deep autoencoder, which maps inputs nonlinearly into a latent representation and reconstructs them. The nonlinear mapping allows the clustering method to address complex structures that may themselves be nonlinear.

The main addition is a self-expressive layer between the encoder and decoder. It brings the self-expressiveness idea from traditional subspace clustering into the network and learns pairwise affinities among all data points. Because the layer is differentiable, those relationships can be learned through ordinary backpropagation together with the surrounding representation.

The authors also introduce pretraining and fine-tuning strategies to learn the network parameters effectively. Their experiments report substantial improvements over the compared leading unsupervised subspace clustering methods. The approach matters because representation learning and learning relationships between examples become parts of the same trainable architecture. The reported results support this integration as a useful way to cluster data with complex structure.
neurips-2017-deep-subspace-clustering-ne.tldr: A differentiable self-expressive layer lets deep autoencoders learn pairwise affinities for improved unsupervised subspace clustering.

paragraphs: Learning from sensitive data creates a tension between useful statistical results and protecting the people represented in the data. The paper studies Bayesian learning with differential privacy when information is distributed across parties, each holding only one or a few samples. This setting makes reliance on a single holder of the complete dataset especially undesirable.

The proposed strategy combines two components with distinct roles. A secure multiparty sum aggregates summaries supplied by data holders, while the Gaussian mechanism provides differential privacy. The aggregation mechanism supports learning from distributed contributions, and the privacy mechanism protects the learning results. Together, they address the centralized trust requirement and excessive noise described for standard approaches.

The strategy builds on Bayesian inference that is asymptotically optimal under differential privacy and practically efficient, with additional cost that diminishes rapidly. The asymptotic qualification matters: it describes behavior in a limiting regime rather than identical performance at every sample size. The contribution brings this inference approach into a setting where the original data remain distributed among many small holders.
neurips-2017-differentially-private-baye.tldr: Secure aggregation and Gaussian privacy noise enable efficient differentially private Bayesian learning from many small distributed datasets.

paragraphs: Mode collapse occurs when a generative model fails to represent the variety of outcomes in the data. This paper proposes D2GAN, which trains a generator against two discriminators to encourage more diverse output. Its objective combines KL divergence and reverse KL divergence, using their complementary statistical properties to capture multiple modes.

The discriminators have opposing preferences: one favors samples from the data distribution, while the other favors generated samples. The generator tries to fool both. The authors show that when the discriminators attain their maxima, optimizing the generator amounts to minimizing both divergences between the data and generated distributions. This theoretical connection is conditional on the optimized discriminators.

Experiments on synthetic data and image datasets including MNIST, CIFAR-10, STL-10, and ImageNet assess sample quality and diversity. The authors report competitive or superior results relative to the evaluated GAN variants, along with an ability to scale to ImageNet. Together, the analysis and experiments support the dual-discriminator objective as a way to address mode collapse while producing good-quality samples.
neurips-2017-dual-discriminator-generati.tldr: D2GAN uses two discriminators and complementary divergence objectives to address mode collapse and improve generated sample diversity.

paragraphs: Stochastic differential equations describe dynamical systems whose evolution includes randomness. Learning about such a system involves estimating both its parameters and its states: the quantities governing its behavior and the system's evolving condition. The paper addresses these two inference tasks together, motivated by their importance across disciplines that model real-world dynamics.

The authors propose a flexible, grid-free algorithm based on variational approximations. The approximation is central to the approach: inference is carried out using an approximate representation rather than being presented as an exact solution. Its scope includes both parameter inference and state inference, so the method addresses uncertainty about the governing model as well as the system being modeled.

Comparisons with leading methods show significant advantages in both runtime and accuracy. Those findings matter because computational efficiency and inference quality are separate practical concerns; the reported method improves both in the comparisons presented. The contribution is therefore an algorithmic approach for stochastic-system inference whose stated evidence combines computational savings with more accurate estimates.
neurips-2017-efficient-and-flexible-infe.tldr: A grid-free variational algorithm jointly supports parameter and state inference for stochastic systems, with reported gains in speed and accuracy.

paragraphs: Linear dynamical systems provide models for data that vary across space and time. Although their modeling capabilities are useful, the space of these systems does not follow ordinary Euclidean geometry. As a result, conventional learning operations cannot simply be applied to their parameters without accounting for that structure.

The paper develops a projected gradient descent method for a general class of loss functions on linear dynamical systems. It first derives a canonical parameter representation, then shows how to compute gradient updates and project them onto the space of valid systems. This representation and projection machinery make optimization compatible with the objects being learned.

The authors apply the method to clustering and sparse coding with linear dynamical systems. They state that their solution avoids approximations both in the system modeling and during optimization, distinguishing it from prior approaches. Experiments report stronger convergence performance and classification accuracy than the compared leading techniques. The contribution is a common optimization procedure that supports multiple learning tasks while respecting the geometry of the models.
neurips-2017-efficient-optimization-for-.tldr: A canonical representation and projected gradient method enable efficient clustering and sparse coding with linear dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Fast accelerators are useful for training models, but their memory may be too small to hold the training dataset. This paper proposes an algorithmic building block for heterogeneous systems, where devices have different storage capacities and processing speeds. Its aim is to make effective use of accelerators such as GPUs and FPGAs even when the data exceed their memory.

The method uses theoretical insights from primal-dual coordinate optimization to decide dynamically which data should be available for fast processing. Its selection signal comes from duality-gap information, connecting data placement to the optimization problem. Instead of treating memory management as separate from learning, the scheme uses information from learning to guide access to limited fast memory.

The approach is designed to adapt to the sizes and speeds within a system's memory hierarchy. In a demonstration involving generalized linear models and a dataset larger than the GPU's memory, the authors report an order-of-magnitude speedup over existing approaches. This result illustrates how optimization-aware data selection can improve training without requiring the full dataset to fit on the accelerator.
neurips-2017-efficient-use-of-limited-me.tldr: Using duality-gap information to select data for fast memory accelerates linear-model training when datasets exceed accelerator capacity.

paragraphs: Sequential data require models to process information across time while learning how one step leads to the next. The Fast-Slow RNN combines two architectural ideas: processing at different timescales and using complex transition functions between successive steps. It brings together strengths associated with multiscale RNNs and deep transition RNNs.

The authors evaluate the architecture on character-level language modeling. They report 1.19 bits per character on Penn Treebank and 1.25 on Hutter Prize Wikipedia, improving the state of the art described in the paper. An ensemble of two models reaches 1.20 on Hutter Prize Wikipedia, outperforming the best known compression algorithm according to that measure.

The paper also empirically investigates learning and network dynamics to explain the improvement over other recurrent architectures. Its design permits any kind of RNN cell as a building block, giving it flexibility beyond a single cell choice. The language-modeling results establish the reported performance gains, while the broader architectural flexibility supports potential application to other sequential tasks.
neurips-2017-fast-slow-recurrent-neural-.tldr: Fast-Slow RNNs combine multiple timescales with complex transitions to improve character-level language modeling.

paragraphs: A classifier can make a confident correct prediction and then become confidently wrong after a small adversarial change to its input. This paper addresses that fragility by deriving formal, instance-specific guarantees. For a particular input, the analysis gives a lower bound on the size of a manipulation needed to alter the classifier's decision.

Such a bound identifies a region of guaranteed decision stability around that input: perturbations smaller than the bound cannot change the decision under the analysis. Because the result is a lower bound, it need not identify the exact smallest successful attack. Its instance-specific form ties the guarantee to the example being evaluated.

The analysis also motivates Cross-Lipschitz regularization, a term intended to improve robustness during learning. The authors apply it to kernel methods and neural networks and report improved robustness without reduced prediction performance. The work therefore links certification with model training: the mathematical analysis supplies both a way to assess stability and a regularizer that improves it in the reported evaluations.
neurips-2017-formal-guarantees-on-the-ro.tldr: Instance-specific robustness bounds motivate a regularizer that improves adversarial robustness without accuracy loss in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can optimize a policy's mean value directly or minimize a Bellman residual, which measures a discrepancy involving its value function and the optimal Bellman update. This paper compares those objectives theoretically and experimentally. It works within policy search, making it possible to study both criteria as objectives over policies.

The authors derive a method that minimizes a weighted absolute Bellman residual over policies. Their theoretical analysis characterizes how well this residual serves as a proxy for policy optimization and finds it better than its value-based counterpart. This comparison concerns the proxy's theoretical properties; it does not establish that residual minimization beats direct value maximization.

Experiments on randomly generated Markov decision processes examine the role of a concentrability coefficient. They find that the residual is generally a poor proxy in those experiments, with direct mean-value maximization performing much better. The result highlights a gap between favorable theoretical proxy comparisons and practical policy quality, raising questions about the widespread use of residual-based objectives in value-based learning.
neurips-2017-is-the-bellman-residual-a-b.tldr: Despite favorable theoretical comparisons with a value-based counterpart, Bellman-residual minimization performs poorly against direct policy-value maximization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find the chordal Markov network structure with the highest score under a given scoring function. This is a search problem over possible network structures. The central challenge is to eliminate unpromising possibilities efficiently while retaining the ability to find the best-scoring structure.

The proposed algorithm combines branch and bound with dynamic programming. Dynamic programming contributes both domain pruning and strong bounds that help prune the search space. These components support the same goal at different levels: reducing the choices under consideration and ruling out regions of the search that cannot improve the solution.

Empirical comparisons show faster runtimes than a recent integer-programming approach, and consequently the constraint-optimization approach discussed in the paper. The method also sometimes handles more variables than a leading pure dynamic-programming algorithm, with potential to reach 20 variables. Its hybrid design avoids the tight exponential memory lower bounds affecting that pure approach. The reported scaling advantage is qualified: it occurs in some cases rather than uniformly across all problems.
neurips-2017-learning-chordal-markov-net.tldr: Combining branch and bound with dynamic-programming pruning improves search for optimal chordal Markov networks and can reduce memory-related scaling barriers.

paragraphs: Accurate object detectors often rely on deep networks whose computation makes real-time use difficult. Compact models can run faster but lose substantial accuracy. This paper develops a framework that transfers information from a teacher detector to a compact detector using knowledge distillation and hint learning, aiming for a better balance between accuracy and speed.

Detection requires more than assigning an image to a class: it also involves regression and region proposals, with less abundant labels. The framework addresses these challenges through several components. A weighted cross-entropy loss handles class imbalance, a teacher-bounded loss addresses regression, and adaptation layers help the compact network learn from the teacher's intermediate distributions.

The authors evaluate different distillation configurations on PASCAL, KITTI, ILSVRC, and MS-COCO. They report consistent improvements in accuracy-speed trade-offs for modern multiclass detectors. These findings support adapting knowledge transfer to the distinct parts of detection, rather than assuming that a method effective for simpler classification tasks will transfer without modification.
neurips-2017-learning-efficient-object-d.tldr: Detection-specific distillation losses and adaptation layers help compact object detectors achieve better accuracy-speed trade-offs.

paragraphs: Embedding Propagation is an unsupervised framework for learning vector representations from graph-structured data. It uses both connections between nodes and information associated with those nodes, such as words or other attributes. The approach learns through communication between neighboring nodes, making graph relationships part of the representation-learning process.

Two kinds of messages drive learning. Forward messages carry representations of node labels or attributes. After these representations are aggregated and evaluated through a reconstruction loss, backward messages carry the resulting gradients. The final node representations are computed from the representations of their labels, linking the learned vectors to the information attached to each node.

An evaluated instance of the framework uses substantially fewer parameters and hyperparameters than the compared methods. Across several benchmark datasets, it is competitive with and often better than leading unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches. The findings suggest that this combination of attribute representations, neighborhood communication, and reconstruction-based learning can provide effective graph representations with a relatively economical model.
neurips-2017-learning-graph-representati.tldr: Embedding Propagation learns graph representations through neighboring attribute messages and reconstruction gradients, achieving competitive results with fewer parameters.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a single rectified linear unit: a weighted sum of inputs that is replaced by zero when negative. Its focus is a high-dimensional setting with fewer observations than weight coordinates. To make learning possible in this regime, the analysis incorporates known structural information about the weights through a closed constraint set.

That set may be convex or nonconvex. The data model is realizable: inputs are independent Gaussian samples, and their labels come from a planted weight vector. Under the studied assumptions, projected gradient descent starting at the zero vector converges to the planted model at a linear rate, with sample requirements optimal up to numerical constants.

The result links structural prior information, sample efficiency, and optimization behavior for a very shallow neural model. Linear convergence means the error decreases geometrically through the iterations covered by the guarantee. The authors suggest that understanding these dynamics may offer insight into deeper networks, while the established result concerns the specified single-ReLU setting.
neurips-2017-learning-relus-via-gradient.tldr: Under structured, realizable Gaussian assumptions, projected gradient descent learns a single ReLU at a linear rate with near-optimal sample requirements.

paragraphs: In a stochastic bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses an arm and observes a random reward. This paper considers problems where the relationship between arms and rewards has known structure. Its framework encompasses many established forms, including linear, Lipschitz, unimodal, combinatorial, and dueling structures.

The authors derive an asymptotic regret lower bound specific to each problem instance. Regret measures the loss associated with choosing less rewarding arms, and the bound describes an unavoidable exploration cost. Their OSSB algorithm matches this limit by targeting the minimum exploration rates for suboptimal arms identified in the lower-bound analysis.

This design differs from optimism-based algorithms and Thompson sampling: exploration is explicitly organized around the rates needed to reach the theoretical limit. Numerical experiments on linear bandits show OSSB outperforming existing algorithms, including Thompson sampling. The theoretical result is asymptotic, while the experimental advantage is demonstrated in the linear setting. Together, these contributions connect a broad structural framework with an exploration strategy derived from its fundamental limits.
neurips-2017-minimal-exploration-in-stru.tldr: OSSB targets theoretically minimal exploration rates and matches an instance-specific asymptotic regret bound for structured stochastic bandits.

paragraphs: Generative moment matching networks compare generated and real samples using maximum mean discrepancy, a kernel-based two-sample measure. Their fixed-kernel formulation has struggled to match GAN performance on challenging datasets and can require large training batches. This paper replaces the fixed Gaussian kernel with adversarial kernel learning to improve expressiveness and computational efficiency.

The resulting MMD-GAN combines moment matching with adversarial learning. The comparison used to train the generator is itself learned, making the discrepancy responsive to differences between the two distributions. The authors describe the resulting distance as a meaningful loss with favorable weak-star topology properties, and show that gradient descent can optimize it using relatively small batches.

Evaluations cover MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA, and LSUN. MMD-GAN substantially outperforms the original moment matching approach and is competitive with representative GAN methods. The findings support learning the kernel as a useful way to improve both the practical training requirements and generative performance of moment matching networks, while retaining a distribution-comparison objective.
neurips-2017-mmd-gan-towards-deeper-unde.tldr: MMD-GAN learns an adversarial kernel to improve moment matching generation and enable training with smaller batches.

paragraphs: Optimizing an expensive black-box function becomes more complicated when cheaper approximations are available. Those sources can save evaluation cost, but their outputs may be biased and noisy. This paper studies how Bayesian optimization can use multiple such sources to find valuable designs while managing the cost of obtaining information.

The proposed algorithm uses a Gaussian-process covariance kernel designed for this setting, together with an acquisition function derived from a one-step optimality analysis. The kernel models relationships relevant to the multiple sources, while the acquisition function guides information gathering. Efficient parallelization supports the computation involved in choosing evaluations.

The authors also introduce a technique that guarantees the asymptotic quality of the algorithm's solution. This is a long-run guarantee, separate from the empirical cost comparison. In experiments, the method consistently finds higher-value designs at lower cost than previous approaches. The contribution combines better modeling of imperfect information sources, a principled evaluation rule, and a quality guarantee for the eventual solution.
neurips-2017-multi-information-source-op.tldr: A Bayesian optimizer combines costly evaluations with cheaper biased sources to find better designs at lower cost in experiments.

paragraphs: Robot motion planning often represents configurations as graph vertices and possible movements as edges. Checking whether an edge is collision-free can be expensive, making the order of checks a major computational decision. This paper focuses on selecting those checks so that a valid path can be found quickly.

The authors connect motion planning to decision region determination, a Bayesian active-learning problem. Directly applying existing methods would require computation exponential in the graph's number of edges. Their BISECT algorithm exploits an explicit assumption: edge validity is modeled by independent Bernoulli random variables. Under this structure, they obtain an efficient, near-optimal algorithm and reduce the stated computational complexity to linear in the number of edges.

Evaluations include mobile robots, manipulators, and real flight data from a full-scale helicopter. BISECT outperforms several leading planning algorithms in these comparisons. The work shows how reasoning about which collision check to perform next can improve planning efficiency, with the independence model providing the key computational simplification behind the proposed method.
neurips-2017-near-optimal-edge-evaluatio.tldr: BISECT selects collision checks efficiently through a near-optimal active-learning formulation that assumes independent edge validity.

paragraphs: Interactive classification usually asks for labels, but comparing two examples may be easier than labeling either one directly. This paper studies a learner that can request both noisy labels and noisy comparisons. A comparison identifies which of two examples is more likely to belong to the positive class.

The central theoretical idea is that access to comparisons reduces the learning problem to learning a threshold function. This lets comparative information help organize the classification task, while label queries still contribute information about the class boundary. The authors develop an interactive algorithm that chooses queries to both information sources.

They analyze the number of labels and total queries required under Tsybakov and adversarial noise conditions for the two oracles. Lower bounds show that the algorithm's label and total query requirements are almost optimal. The result explains when and how an easier form of feedback can reduce the burden of direct labeling, while explicitly accounting for errors in both comparisons and labels.
neurips-2017-noise-tolerant-interactive-.tldr: Combining noisy pairwise comparisons with labels enables interactive classification with nearly optimal label and total query requirements.

paragraphs: Fitting a computational model means searching for parameters that make its behavior agree with data. When model evaluations rely on stochastic simulation or numerical approximation, the search landscape can be complicated and noisy. This paper asks whether Bayesian optimization can become a practical general-purpose tool for this kind of model fitting.

The authors introduce Bayesian adaptive direct search, or BADS, a hybrid Bayesian optimization algorithm. Its design targets competitive optimization performance while keeping the algorithm's own computational overhead affordable relative to typical model runtimes. That balance matters because choosing the next evaluation also takes time, and this cost contributes to the overall fitting effort.

The evaluation compares BADS with many derivative-free, nonconvex optimizers on real-data model-fitting problems from six neuroscience studies. With default settings, BADS consistently finds solutions comparable to or better than those of the alternatives, including vanilla Bayesian optimization. The findings support BADS as a promising broadly useful fitting tool, based on its performance across the tested behavioral, cognitive, and computational neuroscience problems.
neurips-2017-practical-bayesian-optimiza.tldr: BADS combines practical computational overhead with consistently competitive model-fitting results across problems from six neuroscience studies.

paragraphs: Predicting future video frames requires tracking both what a scene looks like and how it changes over time. PredRNN addresses these requirements with a recurrent architecture built around a unified memory for spatial appearance and temporal variation. The goal is to learn the two kinds of structure together from earlier frames.

Its key component is the Spatiotemporal LSTM unit, which extracts and stores spatial and temporal representations simultaneously. Memory is allowed to move vertically across stacked recurrent layers and horizontally through successive recurrent states. This creates a zigzag flow of information rather than keeping memory constrained within each individual LSTM unit.

The authors report state-of-the-art prediction performance on three video-prediction datasets. These results support the proposed memory organization as an effective way to learn spatiotemporal sequences. They also present PredRNN as a general framework that can be combined with other architectures for additional predictive tasks. The demonstrated findings concern video prediction, while architectural integration provides the stated route to broader use.
neurips-2017-predrnn-recurrent-neural-ne.tldr: PredRNN shares spatial and temporal memory across layers and time to improve future-frame prediction.

paragraphs: Calcium imaging records activity from many neurons, but extracting cells and their activity traces requires statistical processing. Imaging data commonly contain substantial contamination from the recording technology or biological tissue. This paper treats that contamination as a central estimation problem and develops a robust approach to recovering neural signals.

Using M-estimation theory, the authors derive a robust loss with a minimax optimality property. They also provide a simple, practical routine for optimizing the loss and prove fast convergence. The statistical objective and its optimization procedure are therefore developed together, addressing both resistance to contamination and the practicality of fitting the model.

The robust loss is incorporated into a matrix-factorization framework that extracts neurons and their temporal activity from imaging datasets. Evaluations on simulated and real data show better performance than existing methods. The contribution is a general robust-estimation treatment of contamination in this setting, supported by theoretical properties of the loss and optimization routine as well as empirical improvements in signal extraction.
neurips-2017-robust-estimation-of-neural.tldr: A theoretically grounded robust loss improves extraction of neurons and activity traces from contaminated calcium-imaging data.
